sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Holocene is the current geological epoch, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago at the close of the last glacial maximum. It is formally classified as the second epoch of the Quaternary period and represents an unusually stable warm interval — an interglacial — within the broader Pleistocene ice age cycles.

In geological terms, the Holocene is remarkably brief, yet it encompasses the entirety of recorded human history and the rise of every major civilization on Earth. Some scientists have argued that humanity's growing impact on Earth's systems warrants designating a new epoch, the Anthropocene, beginning roughly in the mid-20th century.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The defining climatic shift of the Holocene was rapid warming following the retreat of the Pleistocene ice sheets. Global average temperatures rose by roughly 4–5°C compared to the glacial maximum, stabilizing into the relatively mild and consistent climate that characterizes the modern world.

The early Holocene experienced the Holocene Climatic Optimum (approximately 9,000–5,000 years ago), a warm interval when summer temperatures in many regions were 1–3°C warmer than today. Arctic sea ice contracted significantly, and the Sahara Desert was green — a savanna-like landscape dotted with lakes and rivers, home to hippos, crocodiles, and human settlements.

Around 5,500 years ago, changes in Earth's axial tilt weakened monsoon patterns, and the Green Sahara dried out in a relatively rapid transition. Global sea levels rose by approximately 60 metres as the ice sheets melted, stabilizing near present levels around 6,000–7,000 years ago.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The broad continental arrangement of the Holocene is essentially identical to the present day, but the coastlines were significantly different at the epoch's start. With sea levels 60–120 metres lower at the end of the Pleistocene, vast regions of continental shelf were exposed as dry land.

The British Isles were connected to mainland Europe via Doggerland, a low-lying plain that was gradually flooded between 10,000 and 6,000 years ago. The Bering Land Bridge linking Siberia to Alaska persisted into the early Holocene, allowing final pulses of human migration into the Americas.

Australia was connected to New Guinea, and Indonesia's islands were far more connected to the Asian mainland. The Baltic Sea began as a freshwater lake before the breaching of a land barrier connected it to the North Sea around 8,000 years ago.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
As ice sheets retreated northward, vegetation zones followed, dramatically reshaping plant communities across the Northern Hemisphere. Tundra and cold steppe gave way to boreal forest, then temperate deciduous and mixed forest, spreading into regions that had been barren or icy for tens of thousands of years.

The great temperate forests of Europe and North America formed largely during the early and middle Holocene. Grasslands expanded across interior continental regions, and the tropics saw reorganization of forest boundaries as monsoon patterns shifted.

Agriculture, beginning around 10,000–12,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent and independently in China, Mesoamerica, and elsewhere, fundamentally altered plant communities through the domestication and spread of crops. Forests across Europe, Asia, and the Americas were progressively cleared for farmland, a transformation that accelerated dramatically in the last two millennia.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The earliest Holocene witnessed a cascade of megafaunal extinctions that had begun in the late Pleistocene and continued into this epoch. Woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, cave lions, Irish elk, American horses, ground sloths, and the majority of large mammal species in the Americas and Australia vanished — a die-off disproportionately affecting large-bodied animals.

The causes remain debated, but most evidence points to a lethal combination of rapid climate change disrupting habitats and intensive hunting by expanding human populations. Isolated populations of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean until as recently as 4,000 years ago.

Terrestrial megafauna that survived — bison, elephants, rhinoceroses, large bovids — persisted mainly in Africa and southern Asia, regions where animals had co-evolved with modern humans for hundreds of thousands of years and developed stronger flight responses. The Holocene is also notable as the period in which domesticated animals — dogs, cattle, horses, sheep, goats, and pigs — became integral to human civilization.

sections.heading: Human History
sections.body:
The Holocene is entirely coincident with modern Homo sapiens' global dominance. At the epoch's start, humans were skilled hunter-gatherers spread across every continent except Antarctica.

The development of agriculture — independently arising in at least seven to nine regions worldwide — led to permanent settlements, population growth, and eventually the first cities. The Sumerian civilization of Mesopotamia, the Egyptian dynasties of the Nile Valley, the Indus Valley Civilization, and the early Chinese states all arose within the last 6,000 years.

Written language, metallurgy, trade networks, organized religion, and formal governance all developed during this epoch. The industrial revolution, beginning in the 18th century, marks a dramatic acceleration in human modification of Earth's atmosphere, land, and biodiversity — changes that are now inscribed in the geological record and form the primary scientific basis for proposing the Anthropocene as a new epoch.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Mid Pleistocene spans a critical interval in Earth's Quaternary history, roughly from 780,000 to 130,000 years ago. It encompasses several defining transitions: the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, in which glacial-interglacial cycles shifted from 41,000-year rhythms to the dominant 100,000-year cycles that still operate today; the appearance and expansion of Homo heidelbergensis and the first anatomically archaic members of our own lineage; and the rise of some of the most spectacular megafauna the Earth has ever seen.

The Middle Pleistocene was a time of dramatic climatic swings, with ice sheets advancing and retreating repeatedly across the high latitudes, sculpting landscapes and reshaping ecosystems on a continental scale.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Mid Pleistocene is defined climatically by the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT), a fundamental shift in how Earth's ice ages operate. Before roughly 1.2 million years ago, glacial cycles were paced primarily by Earth's axial tilt, running on a roughly 41,000-year cadence.

During the MPT, which concluded around 700,000 years ago, the dominant periodicity shifted to approximately 100,000 years — driven largely by variations in Earth's orbital eccentricity and internal feedbacks within the ice sheet-ocean-atmosphere system. The result was longer, deeper, and more intense ice ages separated by briefer but relatively warm interglacials.

At glacial maxima, ice sheets extended as far south as the northern United States and central Europe, and global mean temperatures were 6–8°C cooler than present. During interglacials, some were warmer than today — the last interglacial before this period, Marine Isotope Stage 11 (~420,000 years ago), may have seen sea levels several metres higher than at present.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Mid Pleistocene geography was broadly similar to today, but coastlines fluctuated dramatically with glacial cycles. At glacial maxima, sea levels dropped by as much as 120–130 metres, exposing vast continental shelves.

The North Sea and English Channel were dry land connecting Britain to Europe. Southeast Asia's Sunda Shelf formed an enormous extension of the Asian continent, connecting what are now Sumatra, Java, and Borneo. In the Southern Hemisphere, the Sahul Shelf linked Australia to New Guinea.

Glaciers gouged the valleys and fjords of Scandinavia, Scotland, Canada, and Patagonia into their recognizable modern forms. The ice itself was massive: the Laurentide Ice Sheet over North America and the Fennoscandian Ice Sheet over Europe were several kilometres thick at their maximum extent, depressing the crust beneath them and raising sea levels globally once they melted.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Vegetation during the Mid Pleistocene tracked the glacial-interglacial cycles closely, with dramatic latitudinal shifts in biome boundaries occurring on timescales of tens of thousands of years.

During cold glacial periods, boreal forest was pushed south into what is now the Mediterranean region, and tundra and cold steppe expanded across vast regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. The mammoth steppe — a productive mosaic of grasses, sedges, herbs, and sparse shrubs — dominated much of northern Eurasia and formed the primary habitat for the great cold-adapted megafauna of the era.

During interglacials, temperate deciduous forest advanced northward, reclaiming areas recently vacated by ice. Grasslands and savannas in Africa and southern Eurasia remained relatively stable refugia through the cycles, supporting diverse grazing and browsing communities.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The Mid Pleistocene megafauna was extraordinary in both diversity and scale. In Eurasia, woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) were evolving from their steppe mammoth ancestors, while straight-tusked elephants roamed the warmer interglacial forests of Europe.

The woolly rhinoceros (Coelodonta antiquitatis) was spreading across northern Eurasia alongside giant deer (Megaloceros giganteus), cave bears (Ursus spelaeus), cave lions (Panthera spelaea), hyenas, and enormous bison.

In North America, mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, American lions, short-faced bears, and a diverse horse fauna dominated the landscape. In Africa, the megafauna was somewhat more similar to today's, though with additional extinct species of hippo, elephant relatives, and large predators. Marine ecosystems supported massive baleen whales and a diversity of large sharks, including the last populations of the enormous Otodus megalodon, which had gone extinct just prior to this interval.

sections.heading: Human Evolution
sections.body:
The Mid Pleistocene is one of the most important chapters in human evolutionary history. Homo heidelbergensis — a large-brained, robust hominin considered ancestral to both Neanderthals and modern Homo sapiens — was widespread across Africa and Europe by 600,000 years ago.

Evidence of controlled fire use dates to this period, with hearths at sites like Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel (~790,000 years ago) and Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa. The earliest known wooden spears, found at Schöningen, Germany, date to approximately 300,000 years ago and reveal sophisticated hunting technology.

In Africa, populations were evolving toward anatomically modern humans, with transitional fossils found at sites like Jebel Irhoud in Morocco (~315,000 years ago). Neanderthals were emerging in Europe and western Asia, adapting brilliantly to cold glacial conditions. The period also saw the first evidence of long-distance raw material transport and the beginnings of symbolic thought, foreshadowing the cognitive revolution to come.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Quaternary, also called the Early Pleistocene, spans from approximately 2.6 million years ago — when the onset of major Northern Hemisphere glaciation marks the formal base of the Pleistocene — to roughly 800,000 years ago, where the Mid-Pleistocene Transition began to reorganize the periodicity of ice ages.

This was the dawn of a new climatic regime on Earth: a world rhythmically pulsing between glacial cold and interglacial warmth, driven by subtle variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. It was also a transformative period in human evolution, witnessing the rise of the genus Homo, the first dispersal of hominins out of Africa, and the development of the earliest stone tool industries. The landscapes of this time were recognizably modern in their broad outlines, yet populated by a strikingly different cast of animals.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Early Quaternary was cooler on average than the preceding Pliocene, but not as dramatically cold as the later Pleistocene glacial maxima. Glacial cycles operated primarily on the 41,000-year timescale associated with variations in Earth's axial tilt (obliquity), and ice sheets, while real and impactful, were generally less extensive than the behemoths of later glacials.

Permanent ice sheets established themselves over Antarctica and Greenland, and seasonal sea ice became a regular feature of the Arctic. Global temperatures were perhaps 1–3°C cooler than the pre-industrial Holocene on average, though with significant oscillations.

Importantly, the closure of the Central American Seaway around 2.8 million years ago — as North and South America joined — dramatically reorganized ocean circulation, strengthening the Gulf Stream and helping drive more moisture into high latitudes. This increased snowfall paradoxically contributed to ice sheet growth in the Northern Hemisphere, triggering the onset of the Quaternary ice ages.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The land masses of the Early Quaternary were positioned very close to their present-day arrangement. The most geologically significant recent event was the completion of the Isthmus of Panama, which formed between 4 and 3 million years ago as volcanic island arcs accreted and the sea floor between North and South America shoaled.

This land bridge divided the single world ocean into separate Atlantic and Pacific basins, profoundly altering global circulation and precipitating the Great American Biotic Interchange — a massive two-way migration of animals across the new land connection.

The Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau continued rising due to the ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, influencing monsoon patterns and atmospheric circulation across Asia. The Alps, Andes, and Cascades were also geologically active and growing during this interval.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The onset of Northern Hemisphere glaciation drove a global reorganization of plant communities. Grasslands and open savannas expanded dramatically, particularly in Africa, Eurasia, and North America, in response to increasing aridity and seasonal drought.

This grassland expansion had profound consequences for the evolution of grazing mammals. Forests retreated toward lower latitudes and were restricted to refugia during cold phases. In Africa, the opening of savanna corridors between forest patches likely influenced hominin evolution by promoting bipedal locomotion and ground-foraging strategies.

In South America, the arrival of North American flora via the Isthmus of Panama introduced new plant families and competed with indigenous South American vegetation. The C4 photosynthetic pathway — a metabolic adaptation that is highly efficient in warm, open, CO2-limited grassland conditions — became increasingly dominant in grasses worldwide during this period.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The Early Quaternary was one of the most dynamic periods in mammalian history, driven both by the Great American Biotic Interchange and the global spread of grassland biomes.

In the Interchange, North American species such as horses, tapirs, peccaries, dogs, llamas, deer, and the great predator Smilodon moved southward into South America. From the south, ground sloths, glyptodonts (enormous armadillo relatives), capybaras, and opossums colonized North America. South American native ungulates and most of the continent's distinctive endemic mammals were eventually outcompeted and driven to extinction over millions of years.

In Africa and Eurasia, early proboscideans, giant pigs, saber-toothed cats (including Homotherium and Megantereon), massive short-necked giraffes, archaic elephants, and diverse bovids populated the savannas. Early Pleistocene seas supported a diverse marine mammal fauna including large sperm whales, early right whales, sea cows, and a rich array of seal and dolphin lineages.

sections.heading: Human Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Quaternary is the crucible in which the genus Homo emerged and first spread beyond Africa. Australopithecines — bipedal but small-brained hominins — were still present in Africa in the early part of this interval, with Australopithecus africanus and the robust Paranthropus lineages coexisting with the earliest Homo.

The transition to Homo habilis, recognized by its larger brain (~600–700 cc) and association with the Oldowan stone tool industry (simple flaked cobbles and choppers), occurred around 2.4–2.3 million years ago.

By 1.9 million years ago, the more derived Homo erectus had appeared — taller, with a larger brain (~900 cc), a more modern body plan, and the more sophisticated Acheulean hand axe technology. Homo erectus was the first hominin to leave Africa, with populations reaching the Caucasus (Dmanisi, Georgia, ~1.85 Ma), Southeast Asia (Java, ~1.7 Ma), and China (Yuanmou, ~1.7 Ma) remarkably quickly in geological terms. This first out-of-Africa dispersal represents one of the pivotal moments in the story of our lineage.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Neogene corresponds to the Pliocene Epoch, the final chapter of the Neogene Period, spanning from roughly 5.3 to 2.6 million years ago. It opened as the Atlantic Ocean flooded back into a desiccated Mediterranean basin, and it closed with the onset of large-scale Northern Hemisphere glaciation that ushered in the Quaternary ice ages.

The Pliocene is often described as the most recent time in Earth's history when global conditions resembled those projected for the coming centuries. Atmospheric carbon dioxide hovered near 350–450 parts per million, global temperatures were 2–3°C warmer than pre-industrial levels, and sea levels stood perhaps 10–25 meters higher than today. For this reason, the epoch is intensively studied as a natural analogue for a warming world.

Continents had nearly reached their modern positions, and many recognizable mammal families were already in place. It was against this backdrop of a slowly cooling, drying planet that the earliest well-documented members of the human lineage walked upright across the woodlands and grasslands of Africa.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The early Pliocene was warm and comparatively stable. The Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period (about 3.3 to 3.0 million years ago) is the best-studied interval: high-latitude regions were dramatically warmer than today, with forests growing on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic, where summer temperatures were perhaps 15–20°C higher than at present. The Greenland ice sheet was greatly reduced or intermittently absent, and the West Antarctic Ice Sheet likely collapsed repeatedly.

The equatorial Pacific may have existed in a persistent 'El Niño-like' state, with a weaker east–west temperature gradient than today. Meridional temperature contrasts between the equator and poles were also shallower, which influenced global wind and rainfall patterns.

From around 3 million years ago, the climate began a long, stepwise deterioration. Declining carbon dioxide, changes in ocean circulation, and orbital forcing combined to push the planet past a threshold. By about 2.7 million years ago, extensive ice sheets were growing across North America and Eurasia, marked in ocean sediments by the first widespread ice-rafted debris — the prelude to the glacial–interglacial rhythm of the Pleistocene.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The world map of the Pliocene was broadly familiar, but several critical gateways were changing shape. The most consequential was the gradual closure of the Central American Seaway as the Isthmus of Panama rose. Its final emergence, commonly placed around 3 million years ago, severed the direct connection between the tropical Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

This closure strengthened the Gulf Stream, carrying more warm, salty water northward into the North Atlantic. Paradoxically, the added moisture may have helped feed the growing Northern Hemisphere ice sheets. On land, the new bridge allowed the Great American Biotic Interchange, a massive exchange of animals between North and South America.

At the very start of the epoch, the Zanclean flood refilled the Mediterranean through the Strait of Gibraltar, ending the Messinian Salinity Crisis during which the sea had largely evaporated. Elsewhere, the Indonesian Seaway narrowed as Australia and New Guinea moved northward, altering the flow of warm water from the Pacific into the Indian Ocean. Mountain building continued in the Himalayas, the Andes, and western North America, reinforcing monsoon systems and rain shadows.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The long Neogene trend toward open landscapes accelerated during the Pliocene. Grasslands and savannas, particularly those dominated by C4 grasses adapted to warm, dry, and seasonal conditions, continued to expand across Africa, South Asia, and the Americas at the expense of closed forests.

In the warm early Pliocene, forests extended much farther poleward than today. Boreal conifer forests of larch, spruce, and pine reached the shores of the Arctic Ocean, and tundra was far more restricted. Mixed temperate forests covered much of Europe, including genera now confined to East Asia or North America, such as Sequoia and Liquidambar.

As cooling intensified toward the end of the epoch, these relict forests retreated, steppe and tundra spread in the north, and the modern biogeographic zonation of vegetation began to take shape. In East Africa, a mosaic of riverine woodland, bushland, and grassland provided the varied habitats in which early hominins lived.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Pliocene faunas were rich and increasingly modern in character. Across the African savannas roamed ancestral elephants, giraffes, rhinoceroses, hippos, a great diversity of antelopes, and three-toed hipparionine horses. They were hunted by saber-toothed cats such as Homotherium and Megantereon, alongside giant hyenas and early members of the lion and leopard lineages.

In the Americas, the rise of the Panamanian land bridge triggered the Great American Biotic Interchange. North American carnivores, camels, horses, and deer moved south, while ground sloths, glyptodonts, armadillos, porcupines, and opossums moved north. South America's native predators, including the flightless 'terror birds' and marsupial saber-tooths, declined in the face of this new competition.

In the oceans, the colossal shark Otodus megalodon persisted through much of the epoch before disappearing around 3.6 million years ago, possibly due to cooling seas, shifting prey, and competition from the emerging great white shark. Baleen whales began their evolutionary trend toward gigantism, exploiting the increasingly productive, seasonally upwelling waters of a cooler world.

sections.heading: Human Evolution
sections.body:
The Pliocene is the epoch of the australopiths. Following the divergence of the human and chimpanzee lineages in the Late Miocene (roughly 7–6 million years ago), the hominin record becomes considerably richer after 4.2 million years ago with Australopithecus anamensis in Kenya and Ethiopia.

Australopithecus afarensis, famous from the 'Lucy' skeleton (about 3.2 million years ago) and the Laetoli footprints of Tanzania (about 3.66 million years ago), was a fully committed biped on the ground, while retaining long arms and curved fingers that suggest continued tree climbing. Its brain was only slightly larger than a chimpanzee's, demonstrating that upright walking evolved long before significant brain expansion.

Other lineages coexisted, including Kenyanthropus platyops and Australopithecus bahrelghazali, as well as the enigmatic 'Burtele foot' hominin. The oldest known stone tools, from Lomekwi in Kenya, date to about 3.3 million years ago. By the close of the epoch, around 2.8 million years ago, the first fossils attributed to the genus Homo appear at Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia, while the robust Paranthropus lineage began to specialize in tough, fibrous plant foods.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Neogene corresponds to the Middle Miocene, a pivotal interval spanning roughly 16 to 11.6 million years ago. It began at the peak of the warmest sustained climate of the past 23 million years and ended after one of the most significant cooling steps in Cenozoic history.

This turning point, known as the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, saw the permanent establishment of a large East Antarctic Ice Sheet and set Earth firmly on the path toward the icehouse conditions of the Plio-Pleistocene.

The interval was a time of extraordinary mammalian diversity. Apes reached their greatest geographic range and variety, spreading across Africa, Europe, and Asia, while grazing mammals, proboscideans, and large carnivores flourished in expanding woodlands and open habitats.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The opening of the Middle Miocene coincided with the Miocene Climatic Optimum (about 17 to 14.7 million years ago). Global temperatures were roughly 5–8°C warmer than pre-industrial levels, and atmospheric carbon dioxide likely ranged between 400 and 600 parts per million. The Antarctic ice sheet was smaller and highly dynamic, and tundra-like vegetation persisted in parts of the Antarctic interior.

The climatic optimum overlapped with the eruption of the Columbia River flood basalts in the Pacific Northwest of North America, which released vast amounts of volcanic carbon dioxide and may have helped sustain the warmth.

Between about 14.7 and 13.8 million years ago, the climate shifted abruptly. Deep-sea oxygen isotope records reveal a major expansion of Antarctic ice and a pronounced cooling of deep ocean waters. Proposed causes include falling carbon dioxide from enhanced silicate weathering and organic carbon burial (reflected in the 'Monterey' carbon isotope excursion), along with reorganizations in ocean circulation. Mid-latitude regions became cooler and more seasonal, and aridity increased across many continental interiors.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Continents were close to their present positions, but several important seaways were still open or in the process of closing. The collision of the Afro-Arabian plate with Eurasia had severed the eastern link between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, eliminating the last remnant of the ancient Tethys Sea as a through-flowing ocean.

In Europe, a large inland sea called the Paratethys stretched from the Alpine foreland to Central Asia. Around 14 to 13 million years ago, it became progressively isolated and fragmented into brackish basins, the forerunners of the Black, Caspian, and Aral Seas.

The Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas continued to rise, strengthening the South Asian and East Asian monsoon systems. In South America, the uplift of the northern Andes reshaped drainage patterns, and the vast Pebas wetland system occupied western Amazonia, home to giant crocodilians and endemic mollusks. Meanwhile, the Drake Passage and Tasmanian Gateway were fully open, allowing the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to thermally isolate Antarctica.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
During the warm climatic optimum, subtropical and warm-temperate forests extended to high latitudes. Broadleaf evergreen forests covered much of southern Europe, and laurel-type forests grew in regions that are now Mediterranean scrubland. Swamp forests of bald cypress and other conifers contributed to the extensive lignite (brown coal) deposits of central Europe.

After the Middle Miocene cooling, vegetation became increasingly partitioned by seasonality. Deciduous trees gained ground over evergreen species in the mid-latitudes, and open woodlands and wooded grasslands expanded in the continental interiors of North America and Eurasia.

Grasses, which had been present for tens of millions of years, became progressively more ecologically dominant. However, most grasslands of this time were still composed of C3 species; the dramatic spread of tropical C4 grasslands would follow in the Late Miocene. The development of more open landscapes had profound consequences for herbivore evolution, favoring animals with high-crowned teeth and long limbs suited to running.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The Middle Miocene hosted some of the most diverse mammal communities ever to exist. In North America, horse diversity reached its peak, with many coexisting genera of three-toed browsing and grazing horses, including Merychippus, which had high-crowned teeth adapted for grinding abrasive grasses. Camels, pronghorns, oreodonts, and rhinoceroses such as Teleoceras shared these landscapes.

Proboscideans had spread out of Africa and diversified widely across Eurasia and North America. Gomphotheres with four tusks, shovel-tusked amebelodonts, and the deinotheres with downward-curving lower tusks represented a variety of feeding strategies. Among carnivores, the bear-dogs (amphicyonids) remained formidable predators, while early cats, hyenas, and the bone-crushing borophagine dogs of North America rose in importance.

In the seas, Otodus megalodon became the apex predator, feeding on the diverse small and medium-sized baleen whales of the time. Raptorial sperm whales such as Livyatan, known from slightly younger deposits in Peru, show that the oceans supported multiple giant predators. Kelp forests, seals, sea lions, and early walruses diversified along the productive margins of the North Pacific.

sections.heading: Ape Evolution
sections.body:
The Middle Miocene was a golden age for hominoids, the group that includes apes and humans. After a land connection formed between Africa and Eurasia, apes dispersed out of Africa and radiated across a warm, forested Eurasia.

In Africa, genera such as Kenyapithecus and Equatorius show adaptations for eating hard foods and for spending time on the ground. In Europe, Pierolapithecus (about 12 million years ago) from Spain displays an upright trunk posture associated with climbing and suspension, a key feature shared with living great apes. Dryopithecus and the recently described Danuvius from Germany (about 11.6 million years ago) suggest that combinations of climbing and upright posture were being explored in diverse ways.

In Asia, Sivapithecus from the Siwalik Hills of Pakistan and India shows facial features that closely link it to the ancestry of the modern orangutan. As the climate cooled and forests became more seasonal toward the end of the Middle Miocene and into the Late Miocene, many Eurasian ape lineages declined. This set the stage for the African origin of the lineages leading to gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Neogene corresponds to the Early Miocene, the opening chapter of the Neogene Period, spanning from about 23 to 16 million years ago. Its base is defined by a brief but significant glacial event at the Oligocene–Miocene boundary, after which the planet entered a prolonged phase of warming that culminated in the Miocene Climatic Optimum.

The Early Miocene was a time of major biogeographic reorganization. The collision of Africa and Arabia with Eurasia created a land bridge that allowed animals to move between continents that had long been separated. This 'Proboscidean Datum Event' brought elephants, apes, and many other African groups into Eurasia, and Eurasian mammals into Africa.

Many of the mammal groups that dominate the modern world — including true cats, dogs, bears, deer, and bovids — appeared or began to diversify during this interval, while several archaic lineages of the Paleogene faded away.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Early Miocene began cold relative to the rest of the epoch. The Mi-1 glaciation, around 23 million years ago, was a short-lived expansion of the Antarctic ice sheet that marks the Oligocene–Miocene boundary in ocean sediment records. Following this event, the climate fluctuated but trended generally warmer.

By the later part of the Early Miocene, the world had entered one of the warmest phases of the past 30 million years. Antarctica retained ice, but the ice sheet was smaller and more variable than today, waxing and waning in response to orbital cycles. Mid- and high-latitude regions enjoyed temperate to subtropical conditions, and sea levels were considerably higher than at present.

The tropics were broad, and the temperature difference between the equator and the poles was much smaller than today. Monsoon systems in Asia and Africa were strengthening in response to mountain building and shifting land–sea patterns, bringing seasonal rainfall that would shape the evolution of ecosystems across these continents.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Continents lay near their modern positions, but important differences remained. Around 19 to 18 million years ago, the Arabian plate made contact with Eurasia, creating the 'Gomphothere land bridge.' This event fragmented the Tethys Ocean, separating the proto-Mediterranean from the Indian Ocean and opening a corridor for terrestrial migration between Africa and Eurasia.

India continued to push into Asia, driving uplift of the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. In East Africa, the first stages of rifting and volcanic uplift were beginning to reshape the landscape, eventually forming the Great Rift Valley that would later play a critical role in human evolution.

South America remained an island continent, separated from North America by the Central American Seaway. Australia continued its slow drift northward, and its interior was still relatively well-watered, supporting extensive rainforests. The fully open Drake Passage sustained the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, keeping Antarctica thermally isolated from warmer oceanic waters.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Warm and humid conditions supported extensive forests across much of the globe. Tropical and subtropical forests extended well beyond their current boundaries, and warm-temperate forests grew at high latitudes in both hemispheres. In Australia, rainforests covered areas that are now arid, as preserved in the fossil sites of Riversleigh in Queensland.

The Early Miocene also saw the continued rise of grasses. While forests were still dominant, open woodlands and grassy habitats were expanding in parts of North America, South America, and Africa. In the Great Plains of North America, grasses were becoming more widespread, influencing the evolution of herbivores with teeth adapted to grinding tougher, more abrasive vegetation.

Kelp forests appeared in the North Pacific during this period, establishing a new and highly productive marine ecosystem. Mangrove swamps and coastal wetlands flourished in tropical regions, supporting diverse invertebrate and fish communities.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
The opening of the Africa–Eurasia land bridge triggered a wave of faunal exchange. Proboscideans, including gomphotheres and deinotheres, spread out of Africa into Eurasia and, soon afterward, reached North America. Moving in the opposite direction, cats, rhinos, pigs, and early bovids entered Africa, profoundly changing its ecosystems.

In North America, a rich fauna included three-toed horses, oreodonts, camels, pronghorns, and the long-necked 'giraffe camels' such as Aepycamelus. Predators included bear-dogs, early canids, and the 'false saber-toothed cats' (nimravids), which were soon joined by true felids arriving from Eurasia.

South America, still isolated, maintained its unique fauna of native ungulates such as litopterns and notoungulates, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts, and marsupial predators, all ruled over by the formidable flightless 'terror birds.' In the oceans, early baleen whales, dolphins, and the first true seals and sea lions diversified, while the megatooth shark lineage was evolving toward Otodus megalodon.

sections.heading: Mammalian Evolution
sections.body:
The Early Miocene was a crucial period for the evolution of primates. In Africa, early apes such as Proconsul, Ekembo, and Morotopithecus lived in the forests of Kenya and Uganda. Proconsul, one of the best-known Miocene apes, lacked a tail but still moved on all fours along branches, showing a mix of primitive monkey-like and derived ape-like traits.

These early hominoids were widespread and diverse in Africa, while Old World monkeys were comparatively rare. This pattern would later reverse, as monkeys came to dominate many habitats while apes declined in diversity.

Beyond primates, the Early Miocene saw the diversification of many modern mammal families. Ruminants such as early deer and bovids began to radiate, carnivorans split into more modern lineages, and rodents and bats continued their extraordinary diversification. The combination of warm climates, new land connections, and changing vegetation created an evolutionary laboratory that shaped the mammalian communities of the later Neogene and beyond.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Paleogene corresponds to the Oligocene Epoch, the final chapter of the Paleogene Period, spanning from about 33.9 to 23 million years ago. Its name, from the Greek for "few new," was coined in the nineteenth century to reflect the relatively small number of modern mollusc species found in its rocks compared with later epochs.

The Oligocene opened with one of the most profound climatic shifts of the entire Cenozoic Era: the Eocene–Oligocene Transition, when the Earth moved decisively from a warm "greenhouse" state into a cooler "icehouse" state and a continental ice sheet became established on Antarctica for the first time.

The world that emerged was drier, cooler, and more seasonal than the lush Eocene. Tropical forests retreated toward the equator, open woodlands and early grass-rich habitats expanded, and many mammal groups underwent dramatic turnover. By the end of the epoch, the foundations of the modern biosphere — including its major ocean currents, polar ice, and many living mammal families — were firmly in place.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Oligocene began with a sharp cooling step known as the Oi-1 glaciation, around 33.7 million years ago. Within a few hundred thousand years, a large ice sheet grew across East Antarctica, global sea level fell by tens of metres, and deep-ocean temperatures dropped by several degrees. Oxygen-isotope records from marine sediments show this event as one of the clearest signals in the Cenozoic climate record.

After this initial plunge, the climate did not continue cooling steadily. The Antarctic ice sheet waxed and waned in response to orbital cycles, and a notable warming phase occurred in the Late Oligocene, around 26 to 24 million years ago, during which the ice sheet may have shrunk considerably. Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, which had been very high during the Eocene, declined through the epoch toward values only a few times higher than pre-industrial levels.

On land, the cooling was accompanied by increasing aridity and seasonality in many continental interiors. Temperature differences between the equator and the poles grew larger than at any previous time in the Cenozoic, setting up the strongly zoned climate belts that characterize the modern world.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The continents of the Oligocene were already close to their present positions, but several key gateways were still in the process of opening or closing. Most significant was the widening and deepening of the Drake Passage between South America and Antarctica and the Tasmanian Gateway between Australia and Antarctica. Together these allowed the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to develop, thermally isolating Antarctica and reinforcing its glaciation.

In the Northern Hemisphere, the Turgai Strait — a seaway that had long separated Europe from Asia — dried up, allowing Asian mammals to flood westward into Europe. India continued its northward collision with Asia, driving the uplift of the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau, while the Alps were rising as Africa pressed against Europe.

The Paratethys, a vast inland sea stretching from central Europe to Central Asia, formed as the older Tethys Ocean was progressively closed off. Falling sea levels exposed large areas of continental shelf, and in North America the Rocky Mountain region experienced widespread volcanism that blanketed the Great Plains with ash, preserving rich fossil beds such as those of the White River Group.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
The cooling and drying of the Oligocene transformed the world's vegetation. The broad belts of paratropical rainforest that had reached into high latitudes during the Eocene contracted toward the tropics, replaced in mid-latitudes by mixed deciduous forests and, increasingly, by open woodlands and scrub.

Deciduous trees such as oaks, beeches, maples, and birches became more widespread in the Northern Hemisphere, reflecting adaptation to seasonal cold. In Antarctica, the once-forested landscapes gave way to cold tundra-like vegetation and, eventually, ice. Conifers and southern beech (Nothofagus) persisted in parts of the Southern Hemisphere.

Grasses, which had existed since the Late Cretaceous, began to become more ecologically important in some regions, particularly in South America and parts of Eurasia. However, the vast grasslands characteristic of the later Neogene had not yet formed; Oligocene "open" habitats were typically a mosaic of woodland, shrubland, and grassy patches.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Oligocene faunas reflected the changing habitats. In the oceans, the cooler, more nutrient-rich waters around Antarctica fuelled a burst of productivity that supported the diversification of modern whales. Both the toothed whales (odontocetes), which evolved echolocation, and the baleen whales (mysticetes), which evolved filter-feeding, appear during this epoch. Penguins also diversified, some reaching sizes far larger than any living species.

On land, a major faunal turnover in Europe known as the "Grande Coupure" (great break) occurred near the start of the epoch, when many endemic European mammals disappeared and were replaced by immigrants from Asia. In Asia and Mongolia, a similar turnover is known as the "Mongolian Remodelling," in which perissodactyl-dominated faunas were replaced by rodent- and lagomorph-dominated ones.

Reptiles and amphibians declined at higher latitudes as temperatures fell, while birds continued to diversify. Among the most striking Oligocene animals were the large flightless birds of South America and the pelagornithids, sea birds with bony tooth-like projections on their beaks and wingspans that may have exceeded six metres.

sections.heading: Mammalian Evolution
sections.body:
The Oligocene was a crucial period for the emergence of many modern mammal lineages. The first true cats (felids), early canids, and the ancestors of bears and seals appeared, alongside the extinct "false sabre-toothed cats" known as nimravids. Among herbivores, early horses such as Mesohippus and Miohippus had three toes and longer legs than their Eocene ancestors, reflecting adaptation to more open terrain.

The epoch is famous for Paraceratherium, a hornless relative of rhinoceroses that inhabited Central Asia and is among the largest land mammals ever to have lived, standing nearly five metres tall at the shoulder. The entelodonts, large pig-like omnivores sometimes called "hell pigs," and the chalicotheres, odd clawed browsers related to horses and rhinos, were also prominent.

Primates retreated from the higher latitudes as forests shrank, but in Africa they continued to evolve. Fossils from the Fayum Depression in Egypt document early anthropoids such as Aegyptopithecus, and the split between Old World monkeys and apes is thought to have occurred late in the Oligocene. Meanwhile, monkeys and rodents appear to have crossed the Atlantic from Africa to South America, likely on rafts of vegetation, founding the lineages of New World monkeys and caviomorph rodents.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Middle Paleogene corresponds to the Eocene Epoch, spanning from about 56 to 33.9 million years ago. Its name, from the Greek for "dawn of the new," refers to the appearance in its rocks of many modern groups of organisms. The Eocene is the longest epoch of the Cenozoic Era, lasting more than twenty million years.

The Eocene began with the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, an abrupt spike in global temperatures, and went on to reach the warmest sustained conditions of the last 66 million years during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. Forests extended to the poles, crocodile relatives lived in the Arctic, and there was little or no permanent ice anywhere on the planet.

Over the course of the epoch, however, the climate gradually cooled. By its close, the Earth was poised on the threshold of the Eocene–Oligocene Transition, when the first major Antarctic ice sheet would form. In between, the Eocene saw the first appearances of many familiar mammal orders, including primates, horses, bats, rodents, and whales.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The Early Eocene was a true "hothouse" world. During the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, roughly 53 to 49 million years ago, global mean surface temperatures may have been 10 to 14 °C higher than today, and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations likely exceeded 1,000 parts per million. Temperature gradients between the equator and poles were remarkably shallow, and polar winters were mild enough to support frost-intolerant plants and animals.

Superimposed on this warm background were a series of shorter "hyperthermal" events — brief episodes of rapid warming associated with large releases of carbon — of which the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum was the largest. Later examples include the Eocene Thermal Maximum 2 and 3.

From about 49 million years ago, the planet began a long-term cooling trend, punctuated by a temporary reversal known as the Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum around 40 million years ago. Declining carbon dioxide levels, changing ocean circulation, and the growing isolation of Antarctica all contributed to this cooling, which ultimately led to the establishment of Antarctic glaciation at the end of the epoch.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
During the Eocene, the continents were broadly recognizable but arranged somewhat differently from today. Australia was still attached to Antarctica, though the two were slowly separating. South America and Antarctica were connected by a land bridge or narrow shelf, and India was colliding with Asia, closing the eastern Tethys Ocean and beginning the uplift of the Himalaya.

Sea levels were high, and shallow seas covered large parts of the continents. The Turgai Strait separated Europe from Asia, and Europe itself was an archipelago of islands, which led to the evolution of many endemic mammal groups. The North Atlantic continued to widen, but land connections across Greenland and Scandinavia and via the Bering region allowed mammals to disperse between North America, Europe, and Asia during parts of the epoch.

In the Arctic, the Arctic Ocean was largely enclosed and at times became so fresh at the surface that the floating fern Azolla bloomed across it in vast mats — the "Azolla event," around 49 million years ago, which may have drawn down significant amounts of carbon dioxide and contributed to later cooling.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Eocene vegetation reflected the extraordinary warmth of the time. Tropical and paratropical rainforests, rich in palms, laurels, and other broad-leaved evergreen trees, extended far beyond the modern tropics. Fossil floras such as the London Clay of England preserve mangrove palms (Nypa) and other plants now found only in tropical Southeast Asia.

At high latitudes, forests flourished even through months of polar darkness. On Ellesmere Island and Axel Heiberg Island in the Canadian Arctic, fossilized stumps of dawn redwoods (Metasequoia) and other deciduous conifers record lush swamp forests growing well north of the Arctic Circle. Antarctica was also forested, with southern beech, conifers, and ferns.

As the climate cooled during the Middle and Late Eocene, these forests began to change. Deciduous and temperate species became more common at higher latitudes, and more open, seasonally dry habitats appeared in continental interiors, setting the stage for the major vegetational shifts of the Oligocene.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
Eocene ecosystems were extraordinarily diverse. Warm waters supported rich reef communities and abundant large foraminifera called nummulites, whose coin-shaped shells are so abundant in some limestones that they were used to build the Egyptian pyramids. Sharks thrived, and the Eocene saw the evolution of many modern groups of bony fishes.

On land, reptiles such as crocodilians, turtles, and large constricting snakes ranged into high latitudes. Birds were diverse, and among the largest predators in some regions were flightless "terror birds" and gastornithids such as Gastornis, a massive ground bird of Europe and North America. Fossil sites such as the Messel Pit in Germany and the Green River Formation in the United States preserve exceptionally detailed records of Eocene life, including insects, fishes, birds, and mammals with soft tissues and even stomach contents intact.

In the seas, one of the most remarkable evolutionary transitions in the fossil record unfolded: the evolution of whales from land-dwelling ancestors. Early forms such as Pakicetus and Ambulocetus lived partly on land, while by the Late Eocene fully aquatic whales such as Basilosaurus and Dorudon patrolled the oceans.

sections.heading: Mammalian Evolution
sections.body:
The Eocene was the epoch in which modern mammal orders came into their own. The earliest undisputed members of the odd-toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, and tapirs) and even-toed ungulates (the group including pigs, camels, and ruminants) appear at its base, spreading across the Northern Hemisphere in the wake of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. Early horses such as Eohippus (Hyracotherium) were small, forest-dwelling browsers the size of a dog.

Primates diversified rapidly, with lemur-like adapiforms and tarsier-like omomyids common in the forests of North America, Europe, and Asia. Bats appear fully formed and capable of flight and echolocation, as shown by exceptionally preserved fossils like Onychonycteris and Icaronycteris. Rodents, too, radiated widely.

Alongside these modern groups, many archaic lineages still flourished. Large herbivores such as the rhino-like brontotheres and the horned uintatheres were prominent, and the carnivorous niches were occupied by creodonts and mesonychids rather than true carnivorans. Toward the end of the Eocene, many of these archaic groups began to decline as cooling and drying transformed their habitats, foreshadowing the large-scale turnover at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Early Paleogene corresponds to the Paleocene Epoch, the first epoch of the Cenozoic Era, spanning from about 66 to 56 million years ago. It began immediately after the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction, in which an asteroid impact near the Yucatán Peninsula, together with massive volcanic eruptions in India, wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and roughly three-quarters of all species on Earth.

The Paleocene is therefore fundamentally an epoch of recovery. In its opening millennia, ecosystems were impoverished and unstable, dominated by "disaster taxa" such as ferns and opportunistic species. Over the following millions of years, however, life rebounded, and the surviving groups — especially mammals and birds — diversified rapidly into the ecological space left vacant by the dinosaurs.

The epoch ended with the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, a sudden global warming event around 56 million years ago that marked the transition into the Eocene and drove further profound changes in the world's biota.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The immediate aftermath of the asteroid impact likely included a brief "impact winter," as dust, soot, and sulphate aerosols blocked sunlight for months to years, collapsing photosynthesis on land and in the oceans. This was followed by a period of warming as carbon dioxide released by the impact and by volcanism accumulated in the atmosphere.

Once conditions stabilized, the Paleocene climate was generally warm and humid, considerably warmer than today, with no permanent polar ice caps. Temperatures fluctuated over the epoch, with a cooler interval in the Middle Paleocene followed by a long warming trend in the Late Paleocene that led into the extreme warmth of the Early Eocene.

Temperature gradients between the equator and the poles were relatively low, allowing temperate forests to grow in polar regions. High sea levels and extensive shallow seas helped moderate climates in many coastal and continental regions.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The continents of the Paleocene were still in the later stages of the break-up of the supercontinent Pangaea. The North Atlantic Ocean was opening, and Greenland was beginning to separate from Europe, a process accompanied by massive volcanic activity that formed the North Atlantic Igneous Province toward the end of the epoch.

India was an island continent moving rapidly northward toward Asia, having recently passed over the hotspot that produced the enormous Deccan Traps lava flows. Australia remained attached to Antarctica, and South America was connected to Antarctica, allowing some faunal exchange across the southern continents.

Shallow seaways still covered parts of the continents. In North America, the Western Interior Seaway that had divided the continent during the Cretaceous had largely drained, though remnants persisted early in the epoch. The Tethys Ocean still separated Africa and India from Eurasia, and Africa itself was an island continent where a distinctive endemic fauna began to evolve.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
Plant life was severely disrupted by the end-Cretaceous extinction. In North America, a pronounced "fern spike" in the fossil pollen record shows that ferns briefly dominated devastated landscapes, as they often do after modern volcanic eruptions. Many plant species, particularly those dependent on specific insect pollinators, disappeared.

As the Paleocene progressed, forests recovered and flowering plants (angiosperms) consolidated the dominance they had begun to achieve in the Cretaceous. Early Paleocene forests were often low in diversity, but by the Middle and Late Paleocene, rich, multi-layered rainforests had developed in places such as Colombia, as shown by the Cerrejón Formation, and in the western interior of North America.

Many modern plant families, including palms, laurels, walnuts, and legumes, were established during this time. Conifers such as dawn redwoods and cypresses grew in swampy lowlands, and deciduous forests spread across the high latitudes, where trees had to cope with long months of darkness during polar winters.

sections.heading: Fauna
sections.body:
With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, the Paleocene world was one of opportunity. Crocodilians, turtles, and champsosaurs (crocodile-like aquatic reptiles) survived the extinction and flourished in rivers and swamps. Snakes also thrived, and the Cerrejón Formation of Colombia has yielded Titanoboa, a giant snake estimated to have reached around 13 metres in length — its size a testament to the warm tropical climate.

Birds, the only surviving dinosaurs, diversified rapidly. Early representatives of many modern bird lineages appeared, and in the absence of large mammalian predators, some birds evolved into large, flightless ground-dwellers. Penguins appeared in the Southern Hemisphere, with early forms such as Waimanu already adapted for swimming.

In the oceans, the extinction had eliminated the great marine reptiles such as mosasaurs and plesiosaurs, as well as the ammonites. Sharks and bony fishes diversified to fill these roles, and the recovery of plankton communities over hundreds of thousands of years gradually restored ocean productivity.

sections.heading: Mammalian Evolution
sections.body:
Mammals had lived alongside dinosaurs for more than 150 million years, but most were small. After the extinction, they underwent an explosive adaptive radiation. Within just a few hundred thousand years of the impact, mammals had increased markedly in body size and diversity, as documented by exceptional fossil sites such as Corral Bluffs in Colorado.

Many Paleocene mammals belonged to archaic groups with no close living relatives. The multituberculates, rodent-like mammals that had flourished in the Cretaceous, remained abundant. Condylarths, a loose assemblage of early hoofed mammals, and pantodonts, heavy-bodied herbivores such as Pantolambda and Barylambda, became widespread. Early carnivorous mammals included creodonts and small, weasel-like relatives of modern carnivorans.

The Paleocene also saw the origins, or early diversification, of lineages leading to modern placental groups, including primate relatives such as the plesiadapiforms. In South America, isolated from other continents, an entirely distinctive fauna of native ungulates and marsupials began to evolve. By the end of the epoch, mammals had become the dominant large land animals, a status they have held ever since.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT) was a major climatic and biological upheaval that took place around 34 million years ago, marking the boundary between the Eocene and Oligocene epochs. It represents the most important step in the Earth's long-term shift from the warm, largely ice-free "greenhouse" world of the early Cenozoic to the cooler "icehouse" world that persists today.

During the transition, which unfolded over roughly 300,000 to 500,000 years in two main steps, a continental ice sheet grew rapidly across Antarctica. Global temperatures fell, sea level dropped, and ocean chemistry shifted, leaving a clear signature in deep-sea sediments around the world.

The EOT was accompanied by significant extinctions and faunal turnovers, both in the oceans and on land. Although less catastrophic than the great mass extinctions, it reshaped ecosystems on a global scale and helped set the course for the evolution of the modern biosphere.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The leading explanation for the transition is a long-term decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide. Proxy records indicate that CO₂ levels fell from well over 1,000 parts per million in the Early Eocene to perhaps around 600 to 800 parts per million by the end of the epoch. Climate models suggest that once CO₂ dropped below a critical threshold, ice sheets on Antarctica could expand rapidly through feedbacks such as increased reflectivity of the ice surface.

The opening of ocean gateways around Antarctica — the Tasmanian Gateway between Australia and Antarctica and the Drake Passage between South America and Antarctica — was once considered the primary cause. As these passages deepened, they allowed the Antarctic Circumpolar Current to develop, which is thought to have reduced the transport of warm water toward the pole. Today, most researchers view gateway changes as an important contributing factor rather than the sole trigger.

Orbital variations also played a role. The final plunge into glaciation appears to coincide with a configuration of the Earth's orbit that produced cool summers at high southern latitudes, allowing winter snow to persist and accumulate. Weathering of newly uplifted mountain ranges, such as the Himalaya, may have further contributed to the drawdown of atmospheric carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: Climatic Changes
sections.body:
The most dramatic climatic change was the rapid expansion of the Antarctic ice sheet, which may have reached a size comparable to, or even larger than, the present-day East Antarctic Ice Sheet. The growth of this ice sheet locked up enough water to lower global sea level by an estimated 50 to 70 metres.

Deep-ocean temperatures fell by several degrees, and the oxygen-isotope composition of benthic foraminifera shifted by more than one part per thousand — one of the largest such shifts in the Cenozoic record. The calcite compensation depth, the level in the ocean below which calcium carbonate dissolves, deepened by more than a kilometre, reflecting major changes in ocean carbon chemistry.

On land, the transition brought cooler temperatures, particularly during winter, and greater seasonality. Many regions experienced increasing aridity. Records from North America suggest that mean annual temperatures fell by several degrees, with winter temperatures dropping even more sharply, and similar patterns of cooling and drying are recorded in Europe and Asia.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
In the oceans, the transition caused extinctions among plankton groups adapted to warm conditions, including many planktonic foraminifera and calcareous nannoplankton. The large, warm-water nummulitid foraminifera that had flourished in the Eocene declined sharply. At the same time, the cooler, nutrient-rich Southern Ocean supported increased productivity, fuelling the diversification of diatoms and, in turn, of the modern groups of whales.

On land, the effects were especially pronounced in Europe, where a turnover known as the "Grande Coupure" saw the extinction of many endemic mammals, including primitive horse relatives and archaic primates. These were replaced by immigrant groups from Asia, such as early rhinoceroses, rodents, and carnivorans, which were able to cross as sea levels fell and the Turgai Strait closed.

In Asia, a similar event, the "Mongolian Remodelling," replaced faunas dominated by perissodactyls with ones dominated by rodents and rabbit relatives. In North America, many reptiles and amphibians declined, and land snail faunas shifted toward drought-tolerant forms. Forests contracted, and vegetation across many continents shifted toward more temperate, deciduous, and open types.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Eocene–Oligocene Transition established the permanent Antarctic ice sheet, which, despite later fluctuations, has persisted in some form for more than 33 million years. It also set up the strong pole-to-equator temperature gradients and deep-ocean circulation patterns that continue to govern the Earth's climate.

Biologically, the transition helped shape the modern world by favouring organisms adapted to cooler, more seasonal, and more open environments. Many of the mammal groups that rose to prominence afterward — including modern carnivorans, ruminants, and rodents — are the ancestors of the dominant mammals of today.

For climate scientists, the EOT is an important natural case study of how the Earth system responds when carbon dioxide levels cross critical thresholds. It demonstrates that gradual changes in greenhouse gas concentrations can trigger abrupt and long-lasting shifts in the state of the climate, offering valuable insights for understanding the potential behaviour of ice sheets in a warming world.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) was a brief but extreme global warming event that occurred about 56 million years ago, at the boundary between the Paleocene and Eocene epochs. Over a geologically short interval, global temperatures rose by an estimated 5 to 8 °C, driven by a massive release of carbon into the ocean and atmosphere.

The event is recognized in sediments worldwide by a pronounced negative carbon isotope excursion — a sharp shift toward lighter carbon — which is used by geologists to define the base of the Eocene. The onset of the warming may have taken only a few thousand years, while the full event, including recovery, lasted around 150,000 to 200,000 years.

The PETM is one of the most intensively studied episodes in Earth's history because it is widely regarded as the closest geological analogue for the ongoing human-driven release of carbon dioxide. It provides a natural experiment showing how the climate, oceans, and life respond to rapid, large-scale carbon emissions.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The PETM was caused by the injection of thousands of billions of tonnes of carbon into the ocean–atmosphere system, but the exact source of this carbon remains a subject of active research. The leading hypothesis links the event to the North Atlantic Igneous Province, a vast episode of volcanism associated with the opening of the North Atlantic between Greenland and Europe. Magma intruding into carbon-rich sediments would have baked out large quantities of methane and carbon dioxide, and evidence of thousands of hydrothermal vent complexes from this time has been found off the coast of Norway.

Additional carbon may have come from the destabilization of methane hydrates — ice-like deposits of methane trapped in ocean-floor sediments — which could have been released as the oceans warmed, amplifying the initial perturbation. Other proposed contributions include the thawing of permafrost at high latitudes, the burning of peat and coal deposits, and the oxidation of organic matter as sea levels changed.

Orbital forcing may also have played a role in timing the event. The PETM occurred during a period of long-term warming in the Late Paleocene, and some researchers suggest that orbital cycles pushed the climate past a tipping point, triggering feedbacks that released carbon from reservoirs that had been primed by the background warmth.

sections.heading: Climatic Changes
sections.body:
Global average surface temperatures during the PETM rose to perhaps 25 °C or more, far above today's value of about 15 °C. Tropical sea-surface temperatures may have exceeded 35 °C, conditions stressful for many marine organisms, while the Arctic Ocean warmed to temperatures resembling those of modern subtropical seas.

The massive influx of carbon caused widespread ocean acidification. In the deep sea, the calcite compensation depth rose dramatically, by as much as two kilometres in some areas, dissolving carbonate sediments and leaving distinctive red clay layers in ocean cores. Oxygen levels in parts of the ocean declined as warming reduced the solubility of oxygen and altered circulation.

The hydrological cycle intensified, with evidence of more extreme rainfall events, increased seasonality, and enhanced erosion in some regions, while others became drier. River systems in places such as the Pyrenees of Spain and the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming show signs of dramatic changes in sediment transport and flooding during the event.

sections.heading: Impact on Life
sections.body:
In the deep oceans, the PETM caused one of the largest extinctions of benthic foraminifera in the last 90 million years, with between 30 and 50 percent of species disappearing. This was likely due to a combination of warming, acidification, and reduced oxygen levels at the seafloor. In surface waters, plankton communities were reorganized, and warm-water species spread toward the poles.

On land, the effects were less a mass extinction and more a massive reorganization. Plants shifted their ranges by hundreds or even thousands of kilometres, as documented in the fossil record of the Bighorn Basin, where subtropical plant species replaced temperate ones during the warmest interval. Insect damage on fossil leaves increased, suggesting that warming boosted insect populations and herbivory.

Mammals were profoundly affected. The PETM coincides with the sudden appearance in North America, Europe, and Asia of three key modern mammal orders: primates, artiodactyls (even-toed ungulates), and perissodactyls (odd-toed ungulates). Their rapid dispersal was likely aided by high-latitude land bridges that became habitable in the warmer climate. Many mammal species also experienced "dwarfing" during the event, with early horses such as Sifrhippus shrinking by roughly a third in body size, possibly in response to higher temperatures and changes in food quality.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The PETM left a lasting mark on the evolution of life. The dispersal of primates, artiodactyls, and perissodactyls across the Northern Hemisphere set the stage for these groups to become some of the most successful and ecologically important mammals of the Cenozoic, and their descendants include humans, horses, cattle, deer, whales, and many others.

The recovery from the PETM also illustrates the long timescales over which the Earth system responds to carbon perturbations. While the initial warming was rapid, it took well over 100,000 years for natural processes, chiefly the weathering of silicate rocks and the burial of organic carbon, to draw down the excess carbon and return the climate toward its previous state.

Today, the PETM serves as a key reference point for understanding modern climate change. Although the total amount of carbon released during the PETM is broadly comparable to what could be released by burning remaining fossil fuel reserves, the modern rate of emission appears to be at least ten times faster. This contrast suggests that current climate change could outpace the adaptive capacity of many ecosystems, making the PETM an important, if sobering, lesson from Earth's deep past.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Cretaceous–Paleogene (K-Pg) mass extinction was a sudden, catastrophic collapse of global biodiversity that occurred about 66 million years ago, marking the end of the Cretaceous period and of the Mesozoic era as a whole. Roughly three-quarters of all plant and animal species on Earth disappeared, including every lineage of non-avian dinosaur, the pterosaurs, the great marine reptiles, and the ammonites that had filled the seas for more than 300 million years.

The event is recorded in rock sequences around the world as a thin layer of clay, often only a centimetre or so thick, known as the K-Pg boundary layer. This clay is anomalously enriched in iridium — an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids — and contains shocked quartz, glassy spherules, and microscopic diamonds, all signatures of a colossal extraterrestrial impact.

The K-Pg extinction is the most recent of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions and by far the most famous. It is one of the sharpest turning points in the history of life: by clearing away the dominant animals of the Mesozoic, it opened the ecological stage for the rise of mammals, birds, and modern flowering-plant ecosystems during the Cenozoic era.

sections.heading: Causes & Triggers
sections.body:
The primary cause of the extinction is now widely accepted to be the impact of an asteroid roughly 10 to 15 kilometres in diameter, which struck the shallow sea covering what is today the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico. The resulting Chicxulub crater, around 180 kilometres across and buried beneath younger sediments, was identified in the early 1990s, confirming the impact hypothesis first proposed by Luis and Walter Alvarez and colleagues in 1980 on the basis of the iridium anomaly.

The impact released energy equivalent to billions of atomic bombs. It struck carbonate- and sulphate-rich rocks, vaporising enormous quantities of sulphur and carbon and injecting them, together with pulverised rock and soot from global wildfires, high into the atmosphere. Tsunamis hundreds of metres high swept the coasts of the proto-Gulf of Mexico, and seismic shaking triggered landslides across the continental margins.

A second contributing factor was the Deccan Traps, a vast outpouring of flood basalts in what is now western India. These eruptions began several hundred thousand years before the impact and continued afterwards, releasing large volumes of carbon dioxide and sulphur gases. Scientists continue to debate the relative contribution of the Deccan volcanism, but most now view the impact as the decisive killing blow, delivered to a biosphere that may already have been under some environmental stress.

sections.heading: Climatic/Environmental Changes
sections.body:
In the hours after the impact, a pulse of heat from re-entering ejecta may have ignited wildfires across large parts of the globe, and the soot from these fires joined the dust and sulphate aerosols spreading through the stratosphere. Within days, sunlight reaching the surface was drastically reduced, producing an 'impact winter' of darkness and cold that may have lasted for several years.

Photosynthesis on land and in the oceans collapsed during this interval. Global average temperatures may have fallen by more than 10 °C, and some models suggest that continental interiors experienced freezing conditions even in the tropics. Sulphate aerosols also returned to the surface as acid rain, which likely acidified the uppermost layer of the oceans and harmed organisms that built shells of calcium carbonate.

Once the aerosols settled out, the longer-lived carbon dioxide released by the impact and by Deccan volcanism drove a period of warming that lasted for tens of thousands of years. Ocean productivity remained depressed for a considerable time — the so-called 'Strangelove ocean' — as the marine food web slowly rebuilt itself from the bottom up.

sections.heading: Biological Impact
sections.body:
The extinction was highly selective. On land, virtually no animal heavier than about 25 kilograms survived. All non-avian dinosaurs perished, as did the pterosaurs. Among birds, the diverse enantiornithines vanished, leaving only a few lineages of ground-dwelling neornithine birds — the ancestors of all living birds. Mammals, lizards, and snakes suffered heavy losses, but small, generalist species with flexible diets fared relatively well.

In the oceans, the ammonites and belemnites disappeared, as did the mosasaurs and plesiosaurs, the last great marine reptiles. Planktonic organisms were devastated: more than 90 percent of calcareous nannoplankton and planktonic foraminifera species went extinct, and reef-building rudist bivalves had already vanished. Organisms that relied on detritus rather than living plants — such as many deep-sea creatures and freshwater animals — survived at noticeably higher rates.

Plant communities were also profoundly disrupted. In North America, the boundary is marked by a 'fern spike', a brief interval in which fern spores dominate the pollen record, reflecting the rapid colonisation of devastated landscapes by hardy pioneer plants before flowering-plant forests recovered.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The K-Pg extinction reshaped the course of evolution. With the dinosaurs gone, mammals underwent an explosive adaptive radiation during the Paleocene and Eocene, rapidly diversifying into the ancestors of primates, hoofed mammals, carnivores, bats, and whales. Birds similarly radiated from a handful of survivors into the thousands of species alive today. Without this event, the lineage that eventually led to humans might never have emerged.

The event also transformed the science of Earth history. The discovery of the iridium anomaly and the Chicxulub crater established that extraterrestrial impacts can cause mass extinctions, overturning a long-standing assumption that geological change is always slow and gradual. It revived interest in catastrophic processes and inspired new fields of research into planetary defence and the monitoring of near-Earth objects.

Today, the K-Pg boundary serves as a benchmark for understanding how ecosystems collapse and recover, and it is frequently invoked in discussions of the present-day biodiversity crisis driven by human activity.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The Late Cretaceous was the final epoch of the Mesozoic era, spanning from about 100.5 to 66 million years ago. It represents the culmination of the Age of Dinosaurs, when some of the most famous prehistoric animals — including Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, and the duck-billed hadrosaurs — roamed the continents.

The epoch was a time of high sea levels, warm global temperatures, and continued fragmentation of the continents. Flowering plants, which had appeared in the Early Cretaceous, rose to ecological dominance, transforming landscapes and forging new relationships with insect pollinators.

The Late Cretaceous ended abruptly with the K-Pg mass extinction, triggered by the Chicxulub asteroid impact. This catastrophe brought an end to the non-avian dinosaurs and many other groups, closing a chapter of Earth's history that had lasted more than 180 million years.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.body:
The early part of the Late Cretaceous was among the warmest intervals of the past quarter-billion years. During the Cenomanian and Turonian stages, around 94 to 90 million years ago, tropical sea surface temperatures may have exceeded 35 °C, and polar regions were free of permanent ice. Forests grew at high latitudes in both hemispheres, and crocodile relatives lived in the Canadian Arctic.

Atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were several times higher than today, sustained by vigorous volcanic activity and high rates of seafloor spreading. The Cenomanian–Turonian boundary was marked by Oceanic Anoxic Event 2, during which large areas of the ocean floor became starved of oxygen, leading to widespread burial of organic-rich black shales.

From the Turonian onward, the climate underwent a gradual cooling trend that continued through the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages. Even so, the world of the latest Cretaceous remained far warmer than the present, with mild conditions extending to high latitudes and only seasonal frost near the poles.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Sea levels during the Late Cretaceous reached some of the highest values of the Phanerozoic, perhaps 100 to 250 metres above today's levels. Shallow epicontinental seas flooded large parts of the continents. In North America, the Western Interior Seaway stretched from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, dividing the continent into two landmasses: Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east.

The supercontinent of Gondwana continued to break apart. South America and Africa had fully separated, widening the South Atlantic, while India drifted rapidly northward as an island continent after splitting from Madagascar. Australia and Antarctica remained joined, and Europe existed largely as an archipelago of islands scattered across a warm, shallow sea.

Toward the end of the epoch, mountain building began along the western margin of North America in an episode known as the Laramide orogeny, which would eventually raise the Rocky Mountains. Meanwhile, the great flood basalts of the Deccan Traps began to erupt in western India shortly before the close of the Cretaceous.

sections.heading: Flora
sections.body:
